# Climate change drove the deep-time assembly of biodiversity

### Paleoatmospheric temperature data

All climate rasters were aligned to a common spatial grid so that each pixel represents the same geographic location through time. Grid cells were retained only when at least one valid observation was present, ensuring that analyses relied on empirical information rather than interpolation alone. For each grid cell, temperature values through time were treated as a time series, and a smooth trajectory was estimated using a generalized additive model (GAM). Spatially explicit reconstructions of mean annual surface temperature across the Northern Hemisphere from 23 to 2 Ma are shown at 1-Myr intervals and 1° × 1° spatial resolution. Each panel represents a single time slice and is displayed using a common color scale to allow comparison across time. These layers form the basis for estimating directional temperature change and climatic instability used in subsequent analyses.

![Paleoatmospheric temperature across the Neogene for North America and Europe](images/clipboard-3710998148.png)

### Obtaining the rate of climate change

Once smoothed trajectories are obtained, temperature change is quantified as the difference between consecutive time steps. These first differences approximate the rate and direction of temperature change through time, allowing spatially explicit assessment of climatic dynamics rather than static climate conditions.

![Paleoatmospheric temperature change in 1Ma](images/clipboard-4291690922.png)

### Estimating climate instability

Climate instability is measured as the standard deviation of mean temperature between consecutive time steps within a moving window of +-2Ma. This captures how variable the atmospheric temperature rather than the warming or the cooling trend. Lower values indicate more stable environments

![\*\*Spatial patterns of paleoatmospheric temperature instability across the Neogene.\*\* Maps show reconstructed paleoatmospheric temperature instability (°C Ma⁻¹) across \*\*North America\*\* (left panel) and \*\*Europe\*\* (right panel) from \*\*22 Ma to 2 Ma\*\*. Each map represents a 1-Ma time slice, illustrating the spatial distribution of temperature variability across the continents. Warmer colors (yellow–red) indicate higher rates of temperature instability, whereas cooler colors (blue) indicate lower instability. Together, the panels illustrate the temporal and geographic variation in climatic instability used in the paleobiogeographic turnover analyses.](images/clipboard-3915710011.png)

## Statistical analyses

#### Spatial binning of fossil locations into fossil paleoassemblages

Fossil occurrences were aggregated into standardized paleoassemblages using a spatiotemporal binning procedure. Records were first assigned to continents and then spatially grouped into regularly spaced bins (\~100 km) to reduce the effects of uneven sampling intensity. Each spatial bin was combined with a discrete temporal bin based on rounded midpoint ages to define unique spatiotemporal assemblages. These paleoassemblages provide comparable units of community composition for subsequent analyses of turnover and paleobiogeographic structure.

![**Paleocoordinates were used to assign fossil occurrences to a discrete grid of hexagonal cells of approximately 100 × 100 km in geographic space**. Fossil occurrences falling within the same grid cell and Neogene stage were grouped into a single paleoassemblage, which served as the fundamental unit for subsequent diversity, compositional, and network analyses.](images/clipboard-320948014.png)

#### Temporal binning of fossil locations into fossil paleoassemblages

![**Temporal distribution of fossil localities across the Neogene.** Bars show the log-transformed number of fossil localities per 1-Myr time bin, plotted against geological time (Ma). The reversed x-axis follows geological convention, with older ages on the left and younger ages on the right, illustrating changes in sampling intensity through time.](images/clipboard-865054988.png)

#### Estimating turnover among fossil paleoassemblages

We estimated compositional turnover among paleoassemblages using genus-level presence–absence data. It first converts the fossil occurrences into a *genus* × *paleoassemblage* incidence matrix, then removes poorly sampled paleoassemblages by requiring a minimum number of observations (`default: >3`). Abundances are reduced to presence–absence to focus on composition rather than counts. Pairwise dissimilarities are then computed among paleoassemblages using the Simpson-based turnover component (`β_SIM`) from the *betapart* framework, yielding a matrix that quantifies the degree of taxonomic replacement (turnover) between all pairs of paleoassemblages.

![**Pairwise compositional dissimilarity across space and time.** Heatmaps show pairwise Simpson dissimilarity (β_SIM) among fossil paleoassemblages for all taxa, herbivores, and carnivores. Colors represent increasing compositional dissimilarity from low (dark) to high (yellow), highlighting differences in turnover structure among trophic groups across spatiotemporal assemblages.](images/clipboard-1792363359.png)

### Sampling intensity

![**Sampling effort was evaluated as the relationship between the number of sampled fossil localities and observed generic richness for every stage in the Neogene**. Sampling–richness relationships were examined within each Neogene stage to assess how efficiently additional localities contributed to the recovery of new genera and to identify stages showing evidence of saturation versus continued sampling dependence.](images/clipboard-2034292060.png)

#### Richness of fossil assemblages rarefied across geological time

Species richness was evaluated within each continent, trophic guild, and time bin using both rarefaction and richness estimation approaches. Fossil occurrence data were split into spatiotemporal subsets (continent × trophic guild × time bin), and for each subset we computed sample-based species accumulation curves (via repeated random permutations) to quantify how observed richness increases with the number of sampled localities. In parallel, we estimated pooled richness for each subset using nonparametric estimators to account for unseen taxa. Outputs from all subsets were then combined into a single data frame containing the number of sites sampled, mean accumulated richness, and uncertainty (standard deviation and standard error across permutations) for direct comparison of sampling completeness and richness trajectories across continents, trophic groups, and time intervals.

![Fossil genus richness across the Neogene and separated by continents and by trophic guilds. Each point represents the asymptote estimates of a rarefaction curve. We show data for two estimates, Jacknife SE-1 (continous lines) and Chao2 (dashed lines).](images/clipboard-3317158724.png)

#### Sensitivity analyses

We tested four model configurations that represent different assumptions about how smooth temperature trajectories are through time. When analyzed together, they provide a sensitivity analysis to understand the impact of different temporal smoothing choices for the shape of temporal climatic trajectories and climate-fossil turnover relationships.

#### Sensitivity of Neogene temperature‐change estimates

-   **gam_6_3 (df = 6, degree = 3):** Allows relatively high flexibility. Temperature trajectories can follow finer temporal variation while remaining smooth, capturing long-term trends as well as moderate shorter-term fluctuations.

-   **gam_4_3 (df = 4, degree = 3):** An intermediate level of smoothing. With fewer degrees of freedom, the model emphasizes broader temporal patterns while still allowing nonlinear trajectories.

-   **gam_4_2 (df = 4, degree = 2):** A more conservative specification. Lower polynomial degree and fewer degrees of freedom produce smoother trajectories that highlight long-term climatic change while reducing sensitivity to short-term variation.

-   **gam_8_3 (df = 8, degree = 3):** The most flexible specification. With more degrees of freedom, the model can track finer-scale temporal changes, allowing the fitted trajectory to follow more detailed fluctuations in the temperature reconstructions.

![\*\*Smoothed trajectories of mean atmospheric temperature across the Neogene under alternative GAM specifications.\*\* Mean atmospheric temperature (°C) from 23 to 2 Ma is shown as smoothed trajectories estimated using generalized additive models (GAMs) with different smoothing parameters (df = 6, degree = 3; df = 4, degree = 3; df = 4, degree = 2; df = 8, degree = 3). Time is shown in millions of years ago (Ma), with older ages to the left. Lines illustrate how alternative smoothing assumptions affect the reconstructed temporal trajectory of temperature used in subsequent analyses.](images/clipboard-2759316063.png)

### Sensitivity of GDM effect estimates

#### Sensitivity to climate change

![**Effects of climate change magnitude on ecological distance under alternative GAM smoothness settings.** Partial ecological distance is plotted against climate change magnitude (°C Myr⁻¹) for mammalian assemblages in North America (top row) and Europe (bottom row), separated by all mammals, herbivores, and carnivores. Curves represent generalized additive model (GAM) smooths fitted with different hyperparameter combinations controlling spline degrees of freedom (df = 4–2, 4–3, 6–3, and 8–3), shown in different colors. Each panel illustrates the fitted response of ecological distance to climate change magnitude for the corresponding continent and trophic grouping under these alternative smoothing specifications.](images/clipboard-545247659.png)
